parsed_answer.content:
In the Spring Framework, both @Component and @Bean are core mechanisms used to register beans within the Spring IoC container, but they operate at fundamentally different levels of abstraction and ownership. The @Component annotation (along with its specialized stereotypes like @Service, @Repository, and @Controller) is a class-level annotation utilized for classpath scanning. When Spring encounters @Component, it automatically instantiates the class based on convention, relying on component-scanning to discover beans without explicit manual configuration. This makes it ideal for application classes where you own the source code.

Conversely, the @Bean annotation is a method-level annotation typically used within a @Configuration class. It gives you explicit, programmatic control over object creation, allowing you to instantiate, configure, and initialize objects whose source code you cannot modify—such as third-party library classes or legacy code. While @Component delegates the instantiation mechanics entirely to Spring's container via classpath scanning and reflection, @Bean forces you to write the exact Java code required to construct the dependency graph, handing the resulting instance over to the container to manage its lifecycle.

rows: Requires ownership of the source class
Can instantiate third-party or unmodifiable classes
Controlled entirely by developer's method body
Easy (can invoke the method multiple times or configure parameterized variants)

items: Classpath scanning with @Component relies on ASM (Bytecode manipulation framework) to inspect classes without loading them into the JVM, improving startup performance.
@Bean methods inside a @Configuration class are intercepted by Spring's CGLIB proxy mechanism to ensure singleton scope semantics are preserved when other @Bean methods cross-reference them.
Using @Component on third-party library classes is impossible because you cannot add annotations to compiled bytecode unless you rely on custom post-processors or bytecode weaving.

parsed_answer.content: A classic interview trap and production gotcha is calling a @Bean method directly from another @Bean method outside of a configuration proxy context. Because Spring intercepts CGLIB-enhanced @Configuration classes, calling another @Bean method returns the existing singleton instance from the container. However, if you place @Bean inside a regular unproxied class (or use lite mode configuration), direct method calls will invoke the constructor repeatedly, breaking singleton scoping and inadvertently spawning multiple unmanaged instances of your dependency.

title: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?
